title: Google's AI Classroom Is Here. Start Asking Questions
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky assesses Google’s roughly hundred education product updates announced at ISTE 2026, arguing districts should both credit what’s useful and ask the questions the announcement skipped. The centerpiece is deep Gemini integration into Google Classroom via three teacher-led tools—Guided Learning (a Socratic tutor on assignments), Study Notebooks (diagnostic quiz plus personalized path), and NotebookLM in Classroom—plus free ACT/GRE/ENEM test prep and a redesigned homepage. He stresses that the genuinely transformative features sit behind higher licensing tiers, that consolidating into Google deepens lock-in and weakens negotiating leverage, and that “actionable insights” dashboards measure engagement, not learning. His core caution: the real test won’t happen in Orlando but in a real classroom in October, and administrators must keep asking which features are included, what the data shows, and what teachers should actually do differently.
points: Google’s ISTE 2026 announcement centers on embedding Gemini into Classroom via Guided Learning, Study Notebooks, and NotebookLM—AI tutoring without a separate app, login, or budget line.
The most transformative features require higher licensing tiers (Teaching and Learning add-on, Education Plus, or AI Pro), which the announcement’s visuals obscure.
Deeper consolidation into Google increases lock-in and reduces a district’s negotiating leverage—the very dynamic that produced the original price increase.
“Actionable insights” dashboards measure engagement and clicks, not whether learning happened, risking teachers drawing exactly the wrong conclusions.

The real test is practical: a teacher in fifth period in October must be able to interpret and act on the data—so administrators should keep asking what features are included and what the insights actually measure.
quotes: Google is too embedded in the Chromebooks, in the logins, in the muscle memory of every teacher who has been assigning work through Classroom since 2019.
It also raises questions that the slides don’t answer and that districts should be asking before they enable any of these features for students.
The question worth asking in your next budget meeting: are we paying for consolidation, or are we paying for capability?
What no dashboard has ever successfully observed is whether any learning happened.
The real test of these announcements will not happen in Orlando. It will happen in a fifth period classroom in October
